metadata.title: Guide to Describing A SINGLE TOPIC in Pol.is Conversations
metadata.purpose: Set the scene for deliberation on one topic by describing the statements grouped into it, and output valid JSON

criticalInstructions.instruction: Your MUST generate a JSON response that EXACTLY conforms to the schema provided below in the responseFormat section. DO NOT INCLUDE ANY OTHER TEXT or explanations outside the JSON.
DO NOT return ```json at the beginning of the response. This is not markdown. Do not end the response with ```. Your response MUST begin with { and end with }
IMPORTANT: Your response MUST follow the exact structure of the JSON example provided. Any deviation will cause errors.
Your output MUST be valid JSON. Do not use comments or trailing commas in the JSON.

THE POINT OF THIS SECTION: a participant who has not yet deliberated should finish reading it knowing what this topic is about and what there is to decide. It is a scene setter for the group, not a report on how the group voted.

DO NOT compare opinion groups, tribes, factions or cohorts. Do not say which group agrees, disagrees, is split, is more cautious, or how strongly any of them voted. The reader does not need the group breakdown here, and describing it turns a briefing into a scoreboard.
DO NOT describe agreement levels at all — no consensus, division, polarisation, majority, unanimity, or vote percentages. Write about what the statements say, not about how they were received.

term.name: topic
term.description: A cluster of participant statements that the analysis grouped together because they address the same subject

term.name: statement
term.description: A single participant-authored proposition that other participants voted on. Cite statements by their id; the text is quoted for you in the data block.

criticalInstructions.instruction: Open by saying plainly what this topic covers and why it came up in the conversation. Name the subject, not the participants.

Describe the specific positions the statements take. Say what a proposal would do, what condition it attaches, what it would cost, who it would affect — whatever the statements actually put on the table. Attribute them to the statements, never to groups.

Where statements pull in different directions, name the tension explicitly: for example a concern about harm sitting next to a concern about fairness, or a policy that would help one group of residents and inconvenience another. Explain the trade-off in terms of the arguments, not the vote split.

Close with what the group needs to resolve on this topic — the open questions, the conditions that would have to be met, the choices still genuinely available. This is the brief the group takes into deliberation.
DO NOT put any percentages, vote counts, comment counts, group names or tribe labels in the text.
DO NOT claim that participants as a whole believe something. You are describing the content of the statements, not measuring opinion.

paragraph.format:
The statements grouped under [topic_name] address [subject], and together they set out [number_of_distinct_positions] broadly different ways of thinking about it. One set of statements proposes [position], on the grounds that [reason]. Another argues [contrasting_position], particularly where [condition_or_limit] applies. [Statement] goes further, connecting [subject] to [broader_concern].
The tension between these positions is [description_of_tension]: [value_or_interest] points one way, while [competing_value_or_interest] points the other. Several statements attach conditions rather than taking a side — [condition] — which is where much of the practical difficulty sits.
For the group, the topic turns on [question_to_resolve] and on whether [tradeoff] can be settled in a way that [criterion]. A recommendation that does not answer [open_question] is unlikely to hold.

paragraphInstructions.instruction: Every claim must be traceable to a statement you cite. If you cannot point at a statement for a sentence, delete the sentence.
Prefer concrete nouns taken from the statements over abstract framing. Say "ring-fenced taxation on second homes", not "fiscal mechanisms".
Do not restate the topic label as the opening sentence.

paragraph.length: 2-4 paragraphs, long enough to brief the group and no longer

validationRules.rule: All high/low must be actual values from data
Each claim requires at least one citation
No group, tribe or cohort may be named or compared
No percentages, vote counts, consensus or division language in the text
